content.p: Of all the countries of Europe, only Scotland has no Hells Angels chapter, according to The Scotsman. The explanation offered in 2007 by the president of the Blue Angels was that his men fought the Hells Angels off. The Blue Angels Motorcycle Club was founded in Maryhill, in the north of Glasgow, in 1963. Its founder's family called it the oldest "one per cent" club in Europe. The press has described a different side: a club of about 200 members in Scotland whose individual members have turned up in courts in Scotland and England, and which the Daily Record says has been linked to organised crime.

The club is not itself a defendant in any of the cases below. Where anyone was convicted or sentenced, it was individuals, and the courts dealt with what those individuals did. This account separates what judges and juries decided from what the press, anonymous sources and the club's own leaders have claimed.
content.h2: From Maryhill rockers to a European club
content.p: The Herald reports that the club was formed in 1963 by Allan Morrison and Billy "Stone" Gordon. The Scotsman, which interviewed the club in 2007, describes it as the work of "a small group of rockers" and says it is reputed to be the oldest outlaw biker gang in Europe. The Herald adds that the club emerged from Glasgow's gang culture, in which various groups were fighting over control of the city's rackets.

The origin of the name is disputed even among those who wear it. The Herald says it is thought to stand for "b*******, lunatics, undesirables and eccentrics", and that others have speculated it came from the colour of the Scottish flag. The Scotsman says the name derives from Scotland's national colours, though some members told its reporter that "Blue" stands for "bastards, lunatics, undesirables and eccentrics".

Its colours matched the myth. The Scotsman described battered leather jackets with "Blue Angels" across the back in Gothic script, a skull with angel's wings between the letters, and a "1%" patch. The patch alludes to a remark attributed to the American Motorcycle Association, that 99 per cent of riders are decent and law-abiding. The Herald adds that the original badge showed a winged skull wearing a German steel helmet, and that the club's patches were sewn onto blue denim.

The club grew beyond Glasgow. The Herald says it had chapters in Scotland, England, Belgium and Spain, and that in the 1970s it began associating with motorcycle clubs in England, forming an alliance with the Road Rats of London. When Morrison died in 2020, the Daily Record counted chapters across Scotland and the north of England, seven in Belgium and two in Spain.

Much of the club's early history rests on what its leaders told reporters. In 2007, Lenny the Lion, then 63 and the president, told The Scotsman that in the 1960s the club had fought bloody battles with rival gangs, mostly Mods, with bar brawls "of John Wayne proportions". Petrol bombs and sneak attacks became normal, he said, until the gangs met and called a truce. He named the Maryhill Fleet as the first rival. He recalled a night in September 1964, when about 300 men on each side fought in the middle of Glasgow and, in his words, "one of us got life in prison for it". The Herald's report on Reynolds's death also records a mass brawl in Glasgow city centre in September 1964 that ended with a Blue Angel sentenced to life. Neither piece names the man or gives the charge.

Reynolds said the Blue Angels fought the Hells Angels in the 1970s, and that this was why they have no Scottish chapter. On violence he told the Scotsman: "Violence is a pillar of our lifestyle." He also said that if someone "f*** with one of us, you f*** with 50 of us".

He claimed a second episode abroad. Four years before the interview, he said, two Blue Angels were shot by another gang in Belgium, and the club "came back and wiped them out. 19 of them were hospitalised." That account comes only from Reynolds. The pages opened here give no police or court record of it, so it stands as the club's own telling, with no independent confirmation. The club's stated policy, in his words, was "Retaliation out of all proportion".

Reynolds was also frank about who could join. A candidate needs two members to nominate him, serves as a "prospect", and then faces a vote of the members. Men in their early thirties were the usual recruits, he said, and members who became heroin users had been thrown out.

The club also turns up at the edge of Glasgow's best-known gangland story. Walter Norval, the leader of the 1970s robbery crew known as the XYY Gang, was jailed for 14 years in 1977, according to the Daily Record. The Glasgow Live history says his daughter Rita married one of the Blue Angels bikers. When Norval died in 2014, aged 85, the Daily Record reported that members of the Blue Angels carried his coffin into Maryhill Crematorium to the sound of the Clash song "Bankrobber". The Herald says some of the club's members were pallbearers there too.
None of the pages opened says the club took part in the XYY robberies. The funeral shows only that the two circles knew each other.

The Blue Angels have shown up as the aggressor or the victim in a run of recorded clashes. Newspaper accounts differ, and they are mostly based on anonymous "sources", so they are reported here as the outlets' claims.

In January 2008, Visordown, citing the Yorkshire Evening Post, reported on an attempted murder trial at Leeds Crown Court. The court heard that Andrew Malham, a director of Thundercity Motorcycles, was shot in the stomach with a crossbow after answering his door at Boston Spa to a caller who said his vehicle had no fuel. The court heard that the defendant Paul Miller, then 32, told him "You're dead, that's it. You're finished" before firing, and the prosecutor said acid was then sprayed through the letterbox. Malham told the court that the trouble began when a number of Blue Angels were prosecuted after a criminal damage conviction following an attack on his home, and the court heard that on 30 April the previous year gang members had passed his business sounding horns and gunning engines on the anniversary of an arson attack. Paul Miller and his brother Andrew both denied attempted murder. The report does not give a verdict.

The Daily Record reported in July 2012 that the Scottish actor and musician Charlie Allan was beaten by two men outside a Stirling hotel. The paper said the attackers were Blue Angels members and that they accused him of helping the Outlaws, a rival club, set up its first Dundee chapter. A source told the paper that two Blue Angels came to warn him off. Allan said the attack had left him "quite traumatised". Police said their inquiries were continuing, and the pages opened here do not report any arrest.

The most serious court case concerned the Nomads, a club founded in Aberdeen in 1966 and thought by the Record to be the biggest biker gang in the north of Scotland. In September 2018, on the A98 near Cullen in Moray, a car driven by Ian Ewing struck the motorcyclist Colin Sutherland. Sutherland, John Sutherland, Edward Forrest and Nicky Syratt were then attacked with a claw hammer, a tyre iron and a baseball bat, BBC Scotland reported. Police found a top bearing the name "Blue Angels" in Ewing's car. The Record said the three other men were airlifted to hospital by Coastguard helicopter.

In February 2020, a jury at the High Court in Edinburgh convicted Ewing, 44, of Stonehaven, of attempted murder and assault. A co-accused, Patrick Noble, was acquitted when the jury returned not proven verdicts, and charges against two other men were dropped earlier. In April 2020, Lady Scott jailed Ewing for seven years, calling the assault "a brutal and planned attack". His lawyer told the court he maintained his innocence.

The Record presented the attack as part of a wider north-east turf war. Its sources called it revenge for Blue Angels members being assaulted earlier that day, and it said the club had tried to gain ground in Aberdeenshire after absorbing the smaller Road Mutts and Tribe gangs over four years. A Nomads source told the paper that the Blue Angels "want to control the north-east", while a Blue Angels source said the Nomads resented small gangs joining the Blue Angels. The Record also noted that Alistair Thompson, described as a senior Nomad, was convicted of a metal-bar attack on two Blue Angels at a petrol station in 2014 and ordered by a sheriff to do 200 hours of unpaid work. Both the Record and the Mirror, which republished the story, said the tensions go back almost 20 years to a fight outside a pub in Old Deer, and that insiders feared the feud could end in a death. That is the papers' reporting of sources, not a finding.

In July 2018, four men in motorcycle club clothing arrived outside a house in Beeston, Leeds, at about 9.30pm. The Yorkshire Evening Post reported that the man inside had left the Blue Angels in 2015; he claimed to have risen to the club's European secretary. He threw his own club's jacket from an upstairs window. The four pleaded guilty to threatening behaviour and were given 12-month community orders. Recorder Richard Thyne said the offence was made worse by the fact that it was planned, committed by a group, in a residential street at night, and that there was a history of bad feeling. The complainant had refused to give evidence.

The newest court case involves a former member. On 8 June 2024, according to BBC News, STV and Glasgow Live, Daniel Laponder, 43, planted a pipe bomb under a van parked outside a house in Lennoxtown, East Dunbartonshire. The van belonged to David Rollo senior, whose son is a Blue Angels member. Laponder had left the club and formed the Mad Dogs Motorcycle Club. The High Court in Glasgow was told the two clubs were "engaged in a feud".

A major incident was declared, the area was evacuated and a 100-metre cordon was held while Royal Navy bomb disposal and other emergency teams attended. Prosecutor Lorraine Glancy KC said the device was a viable pipe bomb. Police traced Laponder through video and social media, and found DNA and fingerprints on items used in the device. At his barge in Kirkintilloch he told officers about a shotgun, which had been shortened. When asked about the bomb he said: "Link the dots. We've been getting attacked all the time." He also said: "I'm not a Blue Angel anymore, I retired a year ago."

Laponder pleaded guilty to wilful fire-raising and to possessing the shotgun without authority. His counsel, John Scullion KC, said motorcycles belonging to friends of Laponder had been set on fire and that a group of bikers had visited his home and threatened him. The judge, Lord Arthurson, deferred sentence for reports and told him he would receive a "significant custodial sentence". The pages opened here do not report the sentence.

Allan Morrison died of COPD in January 2020, aged 77. His family called him "much loved by his friends, family and fellow bikers all over the world". At his funeral on 15 February, police escorted a procession of up to 400 mourners on motorbikes from Maryhill Road to Glasgow Crematorium, while his coffin travelled in a sidecar. Glasgow Live said the mourners came despite torrential rain, from across the world.

Another founder member, the former president Lenny "the Lion" Reynolds, died aged 80, his family announced in January 2026. Members of other Scottish biking gangs posted tributes; Alec Donnelly, of Full Armour MM, wrote of growing up around him as a young boy. The Herald said the funeral would be held in Drumchapel on 17 January, and that bikers were expected to meet at his Dennistoun home to ride with the hearse.
